Family Health

Understanding surgery for cervical cancer

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The name of an operation can hide several different decisions: how much tissue to remove, how to reach it, whether lymph nodes need testing and what this means for future fertility. Cervical precancer and invasive cancer need different plans. A specialist team can explain which options fit your diagnosis and what each is intended to achieve.

What an operation is intended to achieve

Surgery can provide tissue for a diagnosis, help establish how far a cancer has spread, or remove it as treatment. These are different purposes, even when one procedure contributes to more than one of them. After a diagnosis, the team considers the type and extent of disease before recommending an operation.

Surgery is particularly relevant to selected early cervical cancers. It is not automatically the first treatment for every stage, nor a guarantee that cancer cannot return. Some people need radiotherapy with chemotherapy, sometimes with other medicines, rather than a major operation. Your gynaecological-oncology team should explain the aim of the proposed treatment and the reasonable alternatives.

Precancer is different from invasive cancer

Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, often shortened to CIN or described as dysplasia, means abnormal cells in the surface lining. Invasive cancer has grown beyond that lining into deeper tissue. A screening result is a reason for the appropriate investigation; it does not by itself tell you that an invasive tumour is present.

Treatment for precancer can remove an area of tissue, called excision, or destroy the abnormal tissue in place, called ablation. The choice depends on the findings, whether the whole abnormal area can be assessed and whether invasion has been excluded. Ablation leaves no complete specimen to examine, so it cannot simply replace an excision when a tissue diagnosis is needed.

Freezing abnormal cervical cells

Cryotherapy, also called cryosurgery, uses a very cold probe placed against the cervix. The aim is to destroy a suitable area of precancerous tissue by freezing it. It may be performed in a clinic, but availability and eligibility vary between services. It is not a treatment for an established invasive cervical cancer.

A watery discharge, sometimes brown or blood-stained, can continue while the treated surface heals. Ask what amount and duration the clinic expects and how to obtain advice if symptoms change. Follow the instructions about pads, vaginal products and sex. Fever, worsening pain, heavy bleeding or an offensive discharge warrants contact rather than assuming all discharge is normal.

Laser ablation

A focused laser can destroy a selected abnormal surface area through the vagina. This is another ablative technique for appropriate precancer. Local anaesthetic may be used in a clinic, while some procedures take place under general anaesthesia. The setting and pain-control plan depend on the treatment and the person.

The word laser describes the tool, not the purpose of every procedure using it. A laser may also be used to cut out tissue for examination, which is different from vaporising tissue. Ask whether the planned procedure will produce a sample for the laboratory and why that method suits the findings from your examination and biopsy.

Cone biopsy and loop excision

Conization removes a cone-shaped piece of the cervix, including the transformation zone where many abnormal changes begin. A pathologist examines it for the type of abnormality, any invasion and the margins: the edges of the removed tissue. It can therefore establish a diagnosis and, in selected cases, also provide the necessary treatment.

The tissue may be removed with a surgical blade, known as a cold-knife cone, with a laser, or with an electrically heated wire loop. A loop procedure is commonly called LEEP or LLETZ. Some precancers and carefully selected very small cancers can be completely removed this way. The pathology determines whether observation, another excision or further cancer treatment is needed; removal of a visible area does not settle that question by itself.

What a simple hysterectomy removes

A simple or total hysterectomy removes the body of the uterus and the cervix. It does not intentionally remove the surrounding parametrial tissue or an upper segment of vagina in the way a radical operation does. The term total refers to the uterus and cervix; it does not automatically mean removal of the ovaries.

A simple hysterectomy may be suitable for particular very early or low-risk cancers. It is not the routine first treatment for every abnormal screening result or every case of CIN. In selected precancer situations it may be considered after specialist assessment. Lymph-node assessment, when needed for cancer, is a separate component that may accompany the hysterectomy.

When less extensive surgery may be appropriate

The SHAPE trial studied people with early cervical cancer meeting specific low-risk criteria, including tumours no larger than two centimetres and limited invasion. Simple hysterectomy produced a similarly low rate of pelvic recurrence to radical hysterectomy at three years, with fewer urinary problems. Participants also had pelvic lymph-node assessment.

A small tumour alone does not establish that this approach is right for you. The pathology, depth of invasion, imaging and other findings must fit the relevant criteria. Ask whether your cancer qualifies for a less extensive procedure and what uncertainty remains. The trial compared the extent of hysterectomy; it was not designed to settle which surgical route is safest for every simple hysterectomy.

Abdominal, vaginal, laparoscopic and robotic routes

An abdominal operation uses an incision in the front of the abdomen. A vaginal operation removes the uterus through the vagina. Laparoscopy uses a camera and instruments through smaller abdominal incisions, with the removed tissue taken out by an appropriate route. Robotic surgery is a form of laparoscopy in which the surgeon controls instrument arms; the robot does not independently perform the operation.

Not every route is suitable for every cancer operation. Anaesthesia is planned with the surgical and anaesthetic teams and is commonly general for these procedures. The choice should account for cancer outcomes as well as recovery. Avoid choosing solely on incision size, an advertised recovery time or the assumption that a newer tool must be safer.

Radical and modified radical hysterectomy

A radical hysterectomy removes the uterus and cervix together with surrounding tissue, including the parametria and supporting tissues, and an upper portion of the vagina. The exact amount depends on the planned operation and cancer findings; it is not a fixed number of centimetres for everyone. Pelvic lymph nodes are often assessed as part of the overall treatment.

A modified radical procedure removes less surrounding tissue than a more extensive radical operation. Its name alone does not determine which lymph nodes must be removed. Ask the surgeon to describe the intended extent and whether nerve-sparing techniques are appropriate. Removing more tissue can have additional consequences for bladder function and recovery, so the operation should match the disease rather than simply be as large as possible.

Why open radical surgery is generally preferred

For radical hysterectomy in early cervical cancer, the LACC randomised trial found worse cancer outcomes with minimally invasive surgery than with an open abdominal approach. Its final survival analysis, reported in 2024, continued to favour open surgery. Potential short-term advantages such as smaller wounds or a shorter stay must be weighed against that cancer-outcome evidence.

Open surgery is therefore generally the standard approach when a radical hysterectomy is required. Any proposed exception needs a careful specialist discussion about the specific evidence and uncertainties. These findings should not be transferred automatically to a cone biopsy, lymph-node staging or every simple hysterectomy. Ask which research applies to the exact operation proposed for you.

Ovaries, hormones and fertility

Removing the uterus means you cannot carry a pregnancy. Removing the ovaries is a separate decision, affected by the cancer type, age, menopausal status and other planned treatment. Keeping functioning ovaries can preserve hormone production, although surgery or subsequent treatment may still affect ovarian function.

If both ovaries are removed before natural menopause, menopausal symptoms may begin suddenly. Ask about symptom management and whether hormone treatment is suitable in your circumstances. If future parenthood matters to you, request fertility advice before treatment starts. Preserving eggs or embryos may be possible for some people, but feasibility, timing, future options and availability need individual discussion; none guarantees a baby.

Trachelectomy can preserve the uterus

A trachelectomy removes the cervix while retaining the body of the uterus. A radical trachelectomy also removes surrounding tissue and part of the upper vagina. It is considered for selected early cancers when preserving the possibility of pregnancy is important. Imaging, pathology and lymph-node findings help determine whether it is appropriate.

The procedure may use a vaginal or abdominal approach, and some parts, such as node assessment, may be performed laparoscopically. The team reconnects the remaining uterus or cervical tissue to the vagina and usually places a supporting stitch, called a cerclage, near the opening. This does not mean the whole uterine cavity is sewn shut. The exact reconstruction depends on the operation.

Pregnancy after trachelectomy needs specialist care

Retaining the uterus leaves a possibility of pregnancy, not a promise of normal fertility. Narrowing at the new opening, difficulty conceiving, miscarriage and premature birth can occur. After radical trachelectomy, birth is generally planned by caesarean. Discuss these issues before choosing treatment, even if you are undecided about a future pregnancy.

Ask when attempting conception would be appropriate and arrange specialist obstetric advice beforehand. Use contraception until the team advises otherwise. If the removed tissue has an involved margin or lymph nodes contain cancer, further treatment may be needed and can change the fertility plan. Knowing this possibility in advance helps avoid interpreting preservation of the uterus as a guarantee that no other treatment will follow.

What pelvic lymph-node assessment tells the team

Lymph nodes are small immune-system structures that receive fluid through lymphatic vessels. Cancer cells can reach nodes in the pelvis. Examining selected nodes or a larger group helps establish stage and guide further treatment. A pelvic lymphadenectomy or dissection removes nodes from specified areas; it may accompany hysterectomy or fertility-sparing surgery.

Removing nodes can disrupt fluid drainage and cause lymphoedema, including persistent leg or genital swelling. The risk depends on the extent of surgery and other treatment. Report new swelling, heaviness or skin changes so that causes can be assessed and support arranged. Sudden painful swelling, especially with chest pain or breathlessness, needs urgent assessment for a possible blood clot rather than being assumed to be lymphoedema.

Sentinel-node mapping and newer evidence

Sentinel nodes are the first nodes reached along a drainage pathway from the cervix. Mapping uses an injected tracer to locate them. Depending on the service, this may be fluorescent indocyanine green, a blue dye, a radioactive tracer or a combination. The surgeon removes the identified nodes for examination and also assesses suspicious nodes.

Removing fewer nodes may reduce complications, but eligibility and technique matter. The PHENIX trial, published in 2025, supported sentinel-node biopsy alone for selected early-stage patients with negative sentinel nodes, with fewer complications than additional pelvic lymphadenectomy. It does not mean everyone can skip a wider dissection. Ask how the team applies current evidence, what happens if mapping fails on one side, and whether additional tissue will be removed. Detailed laboratory assessment may find disease missed by a rapid intraoperative test.

Para-aortic nodes and changes during an operation

Para-aortic nodes lie higher in the abdomen near the aorta. Sampling or removing them is considered in particular staging situations; it is not a mandatory first step in every radical hysterectomy. The decision depends on imaging, pelvic-node findings and how the information would alter treatment.

If a node test during surgery finds cancer, the team may stop a planned radical hysterectomy and recommend definitive chemoradiotherapy instead. This can avoid the added complications of combining radical surgery with treatments that are already needed. The precise plan depends on where disease is found and the overall stage. A negative rapid result is not the final word: permanent laboratory examination of removed tissue can change the recommendation later.

When pelvic exenteration is considered

Pelvic exenteration is a major operation for a carefully selected group, often with cervical cancer that has returned in the pelvis. The team must assess whether removal is feasible, the likely benefit, alternatives and whether you can manage the recovery. It is not the usual treatment for every recurrence.

The organs removed depend on the cancer’s location and previous surgery. The operation may include reproductive organs, some or all of the vagina, the bladder, the rectum or part of the colon. Anterior, posterior and total exenteration describe different extents. Before consent, ask for a clear explanation or diagram of what is expected to be removed and which reconstruction or diversion is planned.

How urine and stool may leave the body afterwards

If the bladder is removed, a new route for urine is needed. One option uses a short bowel segment as a conduit leading to an opening in the abdominal wall, with urine collected continuously in an external pouch. In selected situations a reservoir can be created and emptied with a catheter. A conduit and a storage reservoir are different arrangements, so neither should simply be described as an ordinary new bladder.

If part of the bowel must be removed, a colostomy may bring the remaining bowel to a stoma on the abdomen, where a pouch collects stool. Sometimes the bowel can be rejoined, but this is not possible or preferable in every case and does not guarantee that no temporary stoma is needed. A stoma nurse can explain care, supplies, clothing and daily activities before surgery.

Vaginal reconstruction and adjustment after exenteration

When vaginal tissue is removed, reconstruction may be possible using suitable skin, bowel or muscle-and-skin tissue. Whether to have it, which technique is suitable and when it can be done are individual decisions. Ask about healing, likely sensation, any ongoing care and alternatives; reconstruction is not a requirement for everyone.

Recovery and adjustment commonly take months and may continue much longer. Fixed six-month or one-to-two-year descriptions cannot predict your experience. Changes in body image, stoma care, energy and intimacy can require practical and emotional support. Sexual desire and pleasure may remain possible, but nobody should be promised that practice alone will restore function or be pressured to resume sexual activity.

Recovery, bladder function and other complications

Hospital stay and time away from usual activities depend on the procedure, route, health and complications. A clinic treatment, a simple hysterectomy and exenteration need very different plans. Smaller-incision surgery may allow earlier discharge in some circumstances, but a short stay does not mean the internal tissues have fully healed.

Possible complications include bleeding, infection, blood clots and injury to the bladder, ureters or bowel. Radical surgery can affect nerves involved in emptying the bladder, and a catheter may be needed while function is assessed or recovers. Discuss pain relief, bowel care, mobility, lifting, work and help at home. Use your own team’s instructions rather than a fixed recovery schedule from another patient’s operation.

Sexual health deserves an individual conversation

The uterus and cervix are not essential for orgasm, so hysterectomy does not automatically remove the capacity for pleasure. That is different from promising that sensation and sex will be unchanged. Pain, vaginal shortening or dryness, altered hormones, fatigue, anxiety and relationship concerns can all affect intimacy.

Treatment may relieve cancer-related pain or bleeding, but that improvement is not guaranteed. Ask when vaginal penetration is safe and seek help for ongoing discomfort. Depending on your treatment, useful support may include lubricants, moisturisers, suitable hormone treatment, pelvic-health care or psychosexual counselling. There is no obligation to recover sexual confidence on a particular timetable.

Results, warning signs and follow-up

The final pathology describes the removed tissue, margins and any involved nodes. It helps determine whether more treatment is recommended, including radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy in appropriate circumstances. Ask when results should arrive, who will explain them and whom to contact if you have not heard. Surgery does not replace ongoing cancer follow-up.

After discharge, contact the team for fever, worsening pain, heavy bleeding, difficulty passing urine or worrying wound changes. Sudden breathlessness, chest pain or collapse needs emergency help. Keep follow-up visits and report new symptoms between appointments. Bring questions about fertility, menopause, swelling, bladder function and emotional recovery as well as the cancer itself.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Surgery should match the stage, pathology and individual priorities. The least extensive suitable treatment is not necessarily the same for every early cancer.

Newer SHAPE and PHENIX evidence supports selected reductions in surgical extent; LACC evidence remains important when choosing the route for radical hysterectomy. Local protocols and eligibility need specialist confirmation.

How BeMama can help

Ask the surgeon to write down the procedure, route, organs and nodes involved, fertility implications, and what could change the plan during surgery.

When to seek help

Follow your surgical team’s recovery instructions. Heavy bleeding, fever, worsening pain or difficulty urinating needs prompt advice; chest pain, sudden breathlessness or collapse needs emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Precancer ablation, excision and invasive-cancer surgery serve different purposes.
  • Simple, modified radical and radical hysterectomy remove different amounts of tissue.
  • The surgical route affects cancer outcomes; smaller incisions are not the only consideration.
  • Fertility-sparing surgery preserves a possibility of pregnancy and still needs specialist follow-up.
  • Node assessment, pathology and recovery support are part of the treatment plan.

Frequently asked questions

Does an abnormal cervical screening result mean I need a hysterectomy?

No. Screening abnormalities need the appropriate assessment. Many precancers are treated with a limited procedure; a hysterectomy is not the automatic next step.

Can a cone biopsy also be treatment?

Yes, for some precancers and carefully selected very small cancers. The laboratory findings, including margins and invasion, determine whether additional treatment is needed.

What is the difference between simple and radical hysterectomy?

Both remove the uterus and cervix. Radical surgery also removes surrounding tissue and part of the upper vagina. Node assessment and ovary removal are additional decisions.

Does a two-centimetre tumour automatically qualify for simple hysterectomy?

No. Size is only one eligibility feature. Pathology, invasion, imaging and other low-risk criteria require specialist assessment.

Is robotic radical hysterectomy always the better option?

No. Randomised evidence found worse cancer outcomes with minimally invasive radical hysterectomy than open surgery. Discuss the evidence for your exact procedure, including any proposed exception.

Will my ovaries always be removed?

No. That decision depends on the cancer, age and planned treatment. Keeping functioning ovaries may preserve hormones, but removing the uterus still prevents carrying a pregnancy.

Can I become pregnant after trachelectomy?

Some people can, but fertility is not guaranteed and miscarriage or premature birth risks may be increased. Pregnancy needs specialist planning, and birth after radical trachelectomy is generally by caesarean.

Can sentinel-node biopsy replace removal of more nodes?

For selected patients it may. Newer trial evidence supports that approach in defined early-stage circumstances, but mapping, pathology and local protocols matter. Suspicious nodes or failed mapping can change the plan.

Does pelvic exenteration always require both a urine and bowel pouch?

No single arrangement applies to everyone. It depends on which organs are removed and which reconstruction is feasible. Ask for a clear explanation of your expected urinary and bowel arrangements.

Will sex be unchanged after surgery?

It may remain pleasurable, but changes in comfort, hormones, sensation, confidence or vaginal anatomy are possible. Ask about healing and support rather than assuming either inevitable loss of pleasure or guaranteed unchanged function.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
